newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Morgan Stanley opens trading desk in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley opens trading desk in Brazil.

text.p: Morgan Stanley & Co opened an equities derivatives desk in Brazil on Tuesday, saying it was bullish on Latin America's largest economy but insuring the new venture for up to $45 million against political risk.
"Morgan Stanley wants to expand dramatically in emerging markets around the world," said Henry A. Fernandez, managing director of Morgan Stanley & Co's Latin American Equity Derivatives Department.

"The question is how do you do it in a way that minimizes your risk? That's what this (insurance) policy is for," Fernandez said at an opening ceremony attended by U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley, who is in Brazil for a hemispheric trade meeting.
The derivatives desk, which will trade options of blue-chip stocks like federally owned Telebras and Petrobras, is Morgan Stanley's first trading operation in Latin America.

The Overseas Private Investment Corp (OPIC), a U.S. government agency that promotes expansion of U.S. businesses abroad, is insuring the venture for up to $45 million in losses. Morgan Stanley will pay an annual premium of $450,000 for the coverge, Fernandez said.
Similar policies are available through private insurers but at a higher cost, he said. The OPIC policy covers currency inconvertibility and state expropriation of privately held assets.

"If for some reason a country decides it wants to nationalize the banking industry, not that Brazil will, or if there is a severe crisis and the currency becomes incovertible, what do you do to cover those risks?" Fernandez asked.
He made it clear that Morgan Stanley would not have opened the derivatives desk in Brazil without the insurance.
"We would have had to figure out another way to trade Brazil, but not in the current structure," he said.

The trading operations will be carried out by Morgan Stanley do Brasil, a wholly owned subsidiary of Morgan Stanley. The Brazilian unit's total assets amount to a little over $100 million, the bulk of which was raised through a medium-term-note program launched last year in Europe.
Steven Magee is executive director of Morgan do Brasil, which has offered investment banking services in Brazil since September of last year.
Just last week Morgan Stanley do Brasil was awarded a contract to draw up a privatization model for Sao Paulo state electricity firm Companhia Paulista de Forca e Luz (CPFL).
On the equities front, Fernandez said Morgan Stanley hoped to become the leader in equity options trading in Brazil. In addition, the firm has requested a broker's license from Brazil's Central Bank.
The license, which Morgan hopes to have by the end of the year, would allow it to underwrite local share offerings and buy local shares for European and U.S. institutional clients.
Morgan Stanley has no immediate plans to trade Brazil's domestic debt and trading of the nation's foreign debt will continue to be handled out of New York, Fernandez said.
